assignments.title: Classical Thinker Profile
assignments.html:
Classical Thinker Profile
SOCIOLOGY HONORS · MAJOR PROJECT · DUE END OF WEEK 8
Assignment60 pointsWeeks 6–8

Overview

You will write a profile of one classical sociological thinker from this course: Aristotle, Tocqueville, Durkheim, Simmel, Tönnies, Nisbet, or Putnam. A thinker profile is not a biography. It is an intellectual portrait. Your task is to explain what problem the thinker was trying to solve, what concepts they built to solve it, and why those concepts still matter for understanding social life.

Focus question

What social problem did your thinker identify, how did they analyze it, and what does their analysis reveal that other approaches to the same problem miss or obscure?

Requirements

Introduction (50 to 75 words). Name the thinker, the historical moment in which they wrote, and the specific social phenomenon their work addresses. Do not write "Durkheim was a French sociologist." Say what he was trying to understand and why it mattered in his own historical moment.

Central contribution (200 to 300 words). Explain two or three key concepts this thinker developed. For each one, define it precisely, including etymology where it illuminates the concept, explain the reasoning behind it, and illustrate it with a concrete example. Write the definitions in your own words. A definition copied from a lesson page does not demonstrate understanding, whatever else it demonstrates.

Contemporary relevance (100 to 150 words). Identify one specific phenomenon in contemporary life that your thinker's concepts illuminate. Do not assert that the ideas "are still relevant." Show it, with a specific example, and explain what your thinker's framework reveals about that example that a different framework would miss.

Conclusion (50 to 75 words). State the most important limitation of your thinker's framework: something it cannot see, a question it cannot answer, or an objection that genuinely challenges it. A sociologist worth reading knows both what a theory reveals and what it obscures. This is not the place to hedge everything you just argued; name one real limitation and let the rest of your argument stand.

Primary source requirement

Your essay must show careful engagement with at least one primary source text by your chosen thinker: a specific claim, argument, or passage you can point to and discuss, not a general impression of "what the thinker believed." Draw this from the primary source guides you have already read for that thinker's week.

If you choose Nisbet or Putnam: neither is available to this course in his own words. Both wrote books still under copyright, so this course does not reproduce or link to them directly. Engage instead with the classical text the course paired with that thinker's week: for Putnam, the Tocqueville reading on civil associations (Primary Source Guide 8B); for Nisbet, the Tocqueville reading on political associations (Primary Source Guide 8A). Explain in your essay how that Tocqueville passage anticipates or supports the modern thinker's argument. This is exactly how the course built those two weeks, so it is not a workaround; it is the intended reading.

If you choose Simmel or Tönnies: neither has a primary-source reading in this course. For these two thinkers only, the Text Study page counts as the primary source: for Simmel, Text Study 4B or 5A; for Tönnies, Text Study 7B. Engage a specific step of the argument the page explains.

About Text Study pages. Text Study 4A, 4B, 5A, and 7B explain a work in Optima's own words. For Durkheim, the primary source comes from Primary Source Guide 3B, 6B, or 7A; Text Study 4A supplies concepts only.

Rubric

Criterion Excellent (18 to 20) Proficient (14 to 17) Developing (10 to 13) Insufficient (0 to 9)
Understanding of the Material (20 pts) Concepts defined precisely, in the student's own words, with accurate historical context. Demonstrates genuine comprehension, not just recognition. Concepts mostly accurate with some minor imprecision. Historical context present but could be developed. Some concepts present but with inaccuracies or reliance on lesson language without paraphrase. Concepts largely absent, inaccurate, or copied from sources without comprehension.
Quality of Reasoning (20 pts) Contemporary example is specific and genuinely illuminated by the framework. Limitation identified is real and shows critical engagement. Contemporary example present but the connection to the framework is somewhat general. Limitation identified but not deeply engaged. Contemporary example is vague or only loosely connected to the thinker's framework. No contemporary example, or the example has no genuine connection to the framework.
Clarity and Precision of Expression (20 pts) Prose is clear, well organized, and economical. Sociological vocabulary used correctly throughout. No grammatical errors that impede comprehension. Mostly clear with some awkward phrasing. Vocabulary mostly correct with occasional imprecision. Organization unclear at points; vocabulary used incorrectly in places. Organization difficult to follow; vocabulary absent or significantly misused.

Total: 60 points.

M365 and file submission

Write in Word. Use MLA or Chicago format as your teacher specifies, and cite the primary source by book and section (for example, Democracy in America II.2.6, or The Division of Labour I.2), not by page number alone.

Save your file in your OneDrive at Optima > Sociology > Sociology_2025-26, following this course's naming rule: LastName_FirstName_ThinkerProfile_SOC12_Final (add _Draft1 for any draft your teacher asks to see first). See the M365 Setup and File Organization Guide if you need a refresher on signing in, folder setup, or submitting through the Canvas OneDrive tab.

assignments.title: Community Institution Study
assignments.html:
Community Institution Study
SOCIOLOGY HONORS · MAJOR PROJECT · DUE END OF WEEK 10
Assignment75 pointsWeeks 9–10

Overview

You will visit and observe a specific community institution: a place of worship, a school cafeteria or school event, a voluntary association, a neighborhood organization, a civic meeting, a local government body, a marketplace, or a comparable public setting. You will write a sociological observation report analyzing what you saw. This is primary field research. Your evidence is what you directly observed, not what you already believe about institutions of that kind in general.

The point of this project is to move past casual observation and learn to see social life the way a sociologist does: noticing patterns, structures, and meanings that are invisible to someone who was not looking for them.

Before you write: the observation

Conduct at least one observation session of at least 45 minutes. You may run several shorter sessions instead if that suits your setting better. During the observation, take detailed notes on:

  • who is present, and how people are arranged in space
  • what activities occur, and what is said
  • what norms appear to govern behavior
  • what kinds of relationships appear to be operating
  • what the physical environment communicates about the institution's purposes and values
  • anything surprising, contradictory, or that raises a question you cannot yet answer

A claim not grounded in something you actually saw does not satisfy the evidence requirement, no matter how sociologically fluent it sounds.

Requirements

Introduction (75 to 100 words). Identify the institution and give the context a reader needs: what kind of institution it is, roughly how many members or participants, how long it has existed. State your thesis: the specific claim about this institution's sociological character that the rest of the report will develop.

Observation description (200 to 300 words). Describe what you observed. Be specific about time, place, number of people, physical setting, activities, and key moments. This section is descriptive, not analytical; save the analysis for the next section. A reader who was not there should be able to picture the scene clearly from what you write here.

Sociological analysis (300 to 450 words). Apply at least four of the following concepts to what you observed: culture, norms, roles, groups, socialization, authority, ritual, social order, or community. For each concept, explain what it means, drawing on course readings, describe a specific observation that illustrates it, and explain what that observation reveals about how the institution functions.

Ground this analysis in at least three theoretical frameworks from the course: for example, what kind of solidarity does this institution produce (Durkheim)? Does it build social capital? Does it represent a form of close-knit community rather than a purely functional association (Tönnies)? Does it develop civic habits (Tocqueville)? Does it serve as an intermediary institution standing between the individual and the state? These are suggestions, not a checklist; any well-applied framework from the course is acceptable, and a single framework will often speak to more than one of your four required concepts at once.

Conclusion (100 to 150 words). Does this institution contribute to community flourishing? What would need to change for it to contribute more effectively? What does your specific observation reveal about the broader sociological condition of institutions of this kind?

Primary source requirement

Draw on at least two primary sources from the course. A primary source is a text printed on a Primary Source Guide page: the thinker's own words, in the public domain. Text Study pages (for example, Weber on bureaucracy in Week 10) and lesson pages are course material on a thinker. They can inform the analysis, but they are not primary sources and do not count toward the two.

Exception: Simmel and Tönnies. Neither has a primary-source reading in the course. For these two thinkers only, a Text Study page counts as the primary source: Simmel, Text Study 4B, 5A, 13A, or 13B; Tönnies, Text Study 7B.

For example, a student observing a worship service might use Durkheim on religious ritual (Primary Source Guide 6B) to explain the function of collective worship; a student observing a school or a civic meeting might use Weber on the types of legitimate domination (9B) or Aristotle on forms of government (9A). Cite each primary source and quote or paraphrase it to show how the thinker's ideas illuminate what you observed. A framework named but never applied to the evidence satisfies neither this requirement nor the Argumentation criterion below.

Rubric

Criterion Excellent (23 to 25) Proficient (18 to 22) Developing (12 to 17) Insufficient (0 to 11)
Quality of Observation (25 pts) Observation description is specific, detailed, and vivid. Particular moments, exchanges, and spatial features are identified. Evidence could not have been produced without actually attending. Observation present with some specific detail but somewhat general in places. Most claims are grounded in observed evidence. Observation description is largely general; specific details present but thin. Some claims appear not directly observed. Observation absent or entirely generic. The report could have been written without visiting the institution.
Application of Frameworks (25 pts) Three or more frameworks applied with precision. Each framework is connected to a specific observed feature. The analysis reveals something not visible without the theoretical lens. Frameworks present but some connections are general rather than specific. Two frameworks fully applied; a third only partially. Frameworks are named but not genuinely applied; the connection to the observations is loose or absent. Fewer than two frameworks applied, or frameworks applied inaccurately.
Argumentation (25 pts) Thesis is clear, specific, and genuinely arguable. Evidence supports the thesis directly. The conclusion draws a non-obvious inference from the analysis. Thesis present but somewhat general. Evidence mostly relevant. Conclusion adequate. Thesis unclear or very general. Evidence loosely connected. Conclusion minimal. No discernible thesis. The report is descriptive only, with no analytical argument.

Total: 75 points.

M365 and file submission

Use Heading 1 and Heading 2 consistently for your section headings (Introduction, Observation Description, Sociological Analysis, Conclusion) and insert a Table of Contents (References tab, Insert Table of Contents) at the top of the document. assignments.title: Sociologist Case Study Reports
assignments.html:
Sociologist Case Study Reports
SOCIOLOGY HONORS · MAJOR PROJECT · DUE END OF WEEK 14
Assignment240 pointsWeeks 11–14

Overview

Over Weeks 11 to 14, write four short analytical reports, one on each of the following sociologists:

  1. Max Weber
  2. Karl Marx
  3. Émile Durkheim
  4. one community theorist of your choice: Tönnies, Nisbet, or Putnam

Each report applies a single concept from that thinker's work to a specific historical event or decision. Suggested cases include the French Revolution, the rise of industrial capitalism, the formation of the American democratic system, or the development of a major religious institution, but any historical case that genuinely fits the thinker's framework is acceptable. Use a different case for each of the four reports.

The goal is not to summarize what happened. It is to show how a sociological lens changes or deepens what we understand about it.

Structure for each report

Concept identification (50 to 75 words). Name the concept and the thinker. Explain the concept precisely, in your own words, with its theoretical context. Why did the thinker develop this concept, and what was it built to explain?

Contemporary application (200 to 275 words). Despite the name, this section is where you apply the concept to your chosen historical case, not a contemporary one. Describe the case clearly, then show specifically how the concept illuminates it. Be concrete: what does the concept let you see that you would not see without it? What features of the case does it explain or predict?

Evaluation (100 to 150 words). What does the concept fail to capture about the case you analyzed? Where does the thinker's framework show its limits? Name one specific thing it does not explain, and identify an alternative framework, from elsewhere in this course, that might address that gap.

Primary source requirement

Each report must engage with at least one primary source by the chosen sociologist, quoting or paraphrasing a relevant passage and explaining how it applies to the case. A primary source is a text printed on a Primary Source Guide page: the thinker's own words, in the public domain. Text Study pages and lesson pages are course material on a thinker. They can inform the report, but they are not primary sources and do not count, with one exception: Tönnies has no primary-source reading in the course, so for a Tönnies report Text Study 7B counts as the primary source.

Report Primary Source Guide
Weber 9B, the types of legitimate domination
Marx 10B, The Communist Manifesto, Chapter I
Durkheim 3B, The Rules of Sociological Method, Chapter I, or 6B, The Elementary Forms of the Religious Life
Tönnies Text Study 7B, Gemeinschaft und Gesellschaft
Nisbet or Putnam 8A or 8B, Tocqueville (8A pairs with Nisbet, 8B with Putnam)

Four reports means four separate primary-source engagements. Reusing the same passage across reports satisfies the requirement for only one of them. For Nisbet or Putnam, neither of whom is printed on a course page in his own words, explain how the Tocqueville reading supports the concept you apply.

Rubric (applied separately to each of the four reports)

Criterion Excellent (18 to 20) Proficient (14 to 17) Developing (10 to 13) Insufficient (0 to 9)
Accuracy and Depth (20 pts) Concept defined correctly and deeply. Context accurate. No errors in the thinker's framework. Concept mostly accurate, minor errors or oversimplifications. Concept partially accurate but with significant errors or thinness. Concept absent, unrecognizable, or attributed to the wrong thinker.
Quality of Application (20 pts) Application specific and illuminating. The concept reveals something not otherwise visible. The historical case is well chosen and accurately described. Application present but somewhat general. Concept connected to the case but the connection is not fully developed. Application vague or primarily definitional. No genuine illumination of the case. No application, or the case described has no real connection to the concept.
Critical Evaluation (20 pts) Limitation identified is genuine and specific. Alternative framework identified and connected to the gap. Shows intellectual honesty and critical engagement. Limitation identified but somewhat generic. Alternative mentioned but not developed. Limitation absent or perfunctory. No genuine critical engagement. No evaluation section, or the section only restates the application without naming any limit.

Each report: 60 points. Total across four reports: 240 points.

M365 and file submission

Write in Word. Organize the document with a clear heading for each of the four reports (Report 1: Weber, Report 2: Marx, and so on), using Heading 1 or Heading 2 consistently so the four sections are easy to tell apart.

Save your file in your OneDrive at Optima > Sociology > Sociology_2025-26. If you submit one combined document, name it LastName_FirstName_CaseStudy_SOC12_Final. If you submit four separate files instead, name each one LastName_FirstName_CaseStudy_[TheoristLastName]_SOC12_Final, following the M365 Setup and File Organization Guide's convention, and upload all four together in the same Canvas submission. Either format is acceptable; what matters is that all four reports arrive together by the Week 14 deadline.

assignments.title: Community Flourishing Capstone
assignments.html:
Community Flourishing Capstone
SOCIOLOGY HONORS · MAJOR PROJECT · DUE END OF WEEK 17
Assignment100 pointsWeeks 15–17

Overview

The Capstone is this course's summative writing project. You will select a community of your choice: a neighborhood, a town, a religious community, a school, an online community, or any other recognizable social group. You will research its key institutions, evaluate their health using the frameworks this course has given you, and propose concrete recommendations for how that community could better support the flourishing of its members.

The guiding question

What does a flourishing community require, and does the community you have studied have those conditions? Where it does, how does it sustain them? Where it does not, what accounts for their absence, and what would restoring them require?

Where this project starts

Your Sociological Journals. The written entries from Weeks 1 to 8 and the video posts from Week 9 on are raw material. Review them before outlining. The strongest Capstones usually build on an observation made early in the course, before the student had the framework to use it fully.

One thread runs through the course. Tocqueville asked what stops a democracy from dissolving into isolated individuals facing a single central power, and answered: the habit of voluntary association. Durkheim asked what binds a society once shared belief has thinned, and traced it to the division of labor and the collective conscience. Tönnies distinguished the close, given bonds of community from the looser, contractual bonds of society. Nisbet argued that the intermediate institutions standing between the individual and the state, family, church, guild, neighborhood, had been systematically weakened. Putnam tried to measure whether that weakening was happening in American life, and found evidence that it was. The five thinkers pose one question: what stands between a single person and the concentrated power of the state, and what happens when it erodes. The chosen community is a place to test that question against evidence, not only against theory.

Requirements

Introduction with thesis (150 to 200 words). Identify the community and give the essential context a reader needs. State a specific, arguable thesis: a claim that could be wrong, supported by specific evidence, about what this community's condition reveals about the sociology of flourishing. A thesis that only describes the community is not yet a thesis.

Theoretical framework section (200 to 300 words). Introduce at least four theoretical frameworks from the course that you will apply. For each, explain briefly why this framework is particularly relevant to the community you are analyzing. This section is your analytical toolkit, not a summary of each thinker's entire body of work.

Evidence and analysis (600 to 900 words). This is the body of the paper. Evaluate at least three of the community's institutions, how families are structured, how authority is organized, how economic life functions, how education and religion operate, how the community handles social change, using the frameworks you introduced above. Draw your evidence from your Community Institution Study, your primary source reading, your Sociological Journals, or additional research. For each institution, assess both its strengths and its weaknesses in contributing to human flourishing, and connect each piece of evidence explicitly to one or more of your frameworks. Show, through specific analysis, how the frameworks illuminate the evidence and how the evidence supports your thesis.

Counterargument (100 to 150 words). Identify the strongest objection to your thesis and address it honestly. A paper that acknowledges no difficulties is not a serious analytical paper. Choose a real objection, not a weak version you can easily dismiss, and let your response to it strengthen your argument rather than merely wave the objection away.

Conclusion (150 to 250 words). Summarize your argument and draw a conclusion about the sociology of community flourishing more broadly. Close with concrete, well-reasoned recommendations for how this community could better support the flourishing of its members, grounded in the sociological theory you have applied, not in personal opinion alone. Name one question your analysis raises that you cannot answer within the scope of this paper.

Primary source requirement

Engage with at least three primary sources from the course, integrating quotations or paraphrases into the analysis rather than dropping them in to satisfy a count. A quotation earns its place only if the paragraph around it could not make the same argument without it.

A primary source is a text printed on a Primary Source Guide page: the thinker's own words, in the public domain. Text Study pages (4A Durkheim on the division of labour, 4B Simmel on the metropolis, 5A Simmel on the stranger, 7B Tönnies on community and society, 10A Weber on bureaucracy, 11B Weber on class, status, and party, 12A Durkheim on the rules of method, 13A Simmel on the metropolis, 13B Simmel on the senses, 14B Weber on the iron cage, 15A Durkheim on moral education) and lesson pages are course material on a thinker. They can inform the analysis, but they are not primary sources and do not count toward the three.

Exception: Simmel and Tönnies. Neither has a primary-source reading in the course. For these two thinkers only, a Text Study page counts as the primary source: Simmel, Text Study 4B, 5A, 13A, or 13B; Tönnies, Text Study 7B.

Rubric

Criterion Excellent (28 to 30) Proficient (22 to 27) Developing (14 to 21) Insufficient (0 to 13)
Thesis and Argument (30 pts) Thesis is specific, arguable, and non-obvious. The argument is coherent and develops the thesis throughout the paper. The conclusion follows from the evidence and framework application. Thesis present but somewhat general. Argument coherent but not fully developed. Conclusion adequate. Thesis unclear or very broad. Argument present but not well organized. Conclusion weak. No discernible thesis. The paper is primarily descriptive, with no sustained argument.
Framework Application (30 pts) Four or more frameworks applied precisely and correctly. Each illuminates specific evidence. Frameworks are used to develop the argument, not just mentioned. Four frameworks present but some applications are general. Most are connected to specific evidence. Fewer than four frameworks fully applied, or frameworks named without genuine application. Frameworks absent or significantly misapplied.
Evidence and Specificity (30 pts) Evidence is specific, drawn from direct observation or research. Claims are grounded. Evidence directly supports the thesis. Evidence present but somewhat general. Some claims not fully grounded. Evidence thin or largely generic. Many claims unsupported. Little or no specific evidence. The paper is primarily theoretical without empirical grounding.
Intellectual Honesty (10 pts) Counterargument is genuine and strengthens the paper. Limits of the analysis are honestly acknowledged. The student names what they do not know. Counterargument present but somewhat formulaic. Some acknowledgment of limits. Counterargument minimal or absent. No acknowledgment of the analysis's limits. No counterargument. The paper presents only one view without critical engagement.

Total: 100 points.

M365 and file submission

Write in Word. Use Heading 1 and Heading 2 consistently across the five required sections, and build a document with Managed Styles so headings stay consistent throughout a long paper. Use Word's Insert Citations and Bibliography tool (References tab) to generate your Works Cited page; this is the one skill moment this course requires by name, because a five-to-seven-page paper with three or more cited primary sources is exactly the case that tool exists for. If your teacher returns a draft with comments, turn on Track Changes (Review tab) before revising, so the revision is visible.

See the M365 Setup and File Organization Guide if you need a refresher on signing in, folder setup, or submitting through the Canvas OneDrive tab.

Sociological Journal 2
SOCIOLOGY HONORS · WEEK 2 · JOURNAL

Prompt

Find one norm you follow at home that you do not follow at school, or one you follow at school that would be strange at home.

Describe both sides precisely. Not "we are more relaxed at home" but the actual behavior: who speaks first, what you wear, whether you ask permission, how you address people, what you do with your phone, when you may leave the table.

Then work through these:

  • Which agent of socialization taught you each one?
  • Did you learn it consciously, or did it simply arrive?
  • What happens if you use the wrong one in the wrong place?

Use at least one of these terms from this week's lessons, and define it in your own words before you apply it: socialization, primary socialization, secondary socialization, agent of socialization, looking-glass self.

What earns full credit

This is scored on completion, but completion means a real attempt on real work. That means:

  • A specific, observable pair of norms, not a generality about home being different from school
  • The term you chose is defined, then genuinely used, not just mentioned
  • 200 to 350 words

Rushed work, a summary of the lesson instead of an observation, or a paragraph that could have been written without doing the reading do not count as completion.

Keep this

Add this entry to the same Word document as Journal 1. By Week 15 the whole set becomes the raw material for your Community Flourishing Capstone, and entries with concrete detail will be worth far more to you then than entries with none.

assignments.title: Sociological Journal 4
assignments.html:
Sociological Journal 4
SOCIOLOGY HONORS · WEEK 4 · JOURNAL

Prompt

Describe a moment when you, or someone you watched, did what Simmel calls taking on the blasé attitude: a deliberate screening-out of some stimulus or social demand.

Be specific about the setting. A corridor, a feed, a shop, a bus, a crowded room. Then say what was being screened out, and how you could tell it was being screened rather than simply missed.

Now apply Simmel's analysis, and this is the part that matters:

  • Was the detachment protection or loss?
  • Was something worth attending to screened out along with the noise?
  • Could the person have kept the protection without the cost, or do they come together?

What earns full credit

Simmel's position is genuinely ambivalent and the strongest responses keep it that way. The city is liberating and alienating at once. The blasé attitude is adaptive and it is costly. An answer that resolves cleanly into "detachment is bad" or "you have to filter, so it is fine" has dropped half the argument.

Note also what Simmel does not say. He does not call the blasé attitude a character flaw. He calls the intellect a protective organ, which is the language of biology, not of complaint. If your entry reads as a criticism of the person, reread that phrase and try again.

This is scored on completion, and completion means a real attempt on real work: a specific observed moment, both sides of the ambivalence, and 200 to 350 words.

Keep this

Add this entry to the same Word document as Journals 1 to 3. This is your fourth. In Week 15 the Capstone draws on the whole journal, and a journal with four concrete observations in it gives it far more to work with than a journal with four summaries.

assignments.title: Sociological Journal 6
assignments.html:
Sociological Journal 6
SOCIOLOGY HONORS · WEEK 6 · JOURNAL

Prompt

Identify a ritual, religious or secular, that you have participated in or observed.

Analyze it using Durkheim's framework:

  • What is sacred in this ritual? Name the object, symbol, or moment that is treated as set apart from the ordinary.
  • What is the ritual doing socially? What kind of solidarity does it produce or reinforce?
  • Does the ritual require shared belief to work, or does it produce its effect even for participants who do not fully believe?

Write 200 to 350 words. You may analyze a religious ritual or a secular one (a graduation ceremony, a national holiday, a sporting event). The sociological question is the same in either case.

What earns full credit

This is scored on completion, but completion means a real attempt on real work. That means:

  • A specific, named ritual you actually observed or took part in, not a generic description of "rituals" in the abstract
  • All three prompts addressed, with the sacred element named precisely rather than gestured at
  • 200 to 350 words

Rushed work, a summary of the lesson instead of an observation, or a paragraph that could have been written without doing the reading do not count as completion.

Keep this

Add this entry to the same Word document as your earlier journal entries. By Week 15 the whole set becomes the raw material for your Community Flourishing Capstone, and an entry naming a real ritual with real detail will be worth far more to you then than a generic one.

assignments.title: Sociological Journal 8
assignments.html:
Sociological Journal 8
SOCIOLOGY HONORS · WEEK 8 · JOURNAL

Prompt

Putnam's argument depends on the claim that social capital is declining. Based on your own observations and experience, do you agree?

Identify two forms of social capital you observe in your own community: one that seems healthy and one that seems depleted. Use the distinction between bonding and bridging social capital from Lesson 8.02 in your analysis.

Write 200 to 350 words. Be as specific as possible: name the actual networks, organizations, or forms of trust you are observing, not generic claims about "society."

What earns full credit

The strongest entries name a real, specific association or network the writer actually belongs to or has directly observed, not an abstraction. "My neighborhood has weak social capital" is a claim. "The tenants' association on my street stopped meeting two years ago and nobody has organized a replacement" is an observation.

Use the bonding/bridging distinction to do real work, not just to attach a label. A strong entry says which kind of capital is healthy or depleted and why that distinction matters for the example chosen, not only which box the example goes in.

This is scored on completion, and completion means a real attempt on real work: two specific, named examples, the bonding/bridging distinction genuinely applied, and 200 to 350 words.

Keep this

Add this entry to the same Word document as Journals 1 through 7. This is your eighth entry, and the Capstone in Week 15 draws on the whole journal. An entry with a concrete example in it will be far easier to return to than one that only summarizes the reading.

discussions.title: Sociological Journal 1
discussions.html:
Sociological Journal 1
SOCIOLOGY HONORS · WEEK 1 · JOURNAL

Prompt

Choose one social rule or expectation you ran into today and had not questioned until now. It might be small: how you greet a teacher, how you sit in class, what you wear in a particular setting, who speaks first in a conversation.

Describe it precisely. Then work through these questions in your entry:

  • Where did this rule come from?
  • Did you choose it?
  • Could you break it easily?
  • What would actually happen if you did?

Connect your observation explicitly to one idea from this week's lessons: either Aristotle's claim that human beings are social by nature, or Hobbes's claim that social rules hold only because something enforces them.

Do not summarize the lesson. Apply the idea to what you actually observed.

Peer response

Read one classmate's entry and reply. Your reply should do one of two things: name a way their observation supports the thinker they chose, or name a way it fits the other thinker better. Say which and explain why. A reply that only agrees does not count.

Scoring

Level Criteria
Full credit A specific, precisely described observation; explicit and accurate use of Aristotle or Hobbes; a substantive peer reply
Partial credit Observation is vague or generic, or the thinker is named but not really applied, or the peer reply is thin
No credit Missing, off-task, a summary of the lesson rather than an observation, or no peer reply

discussions.title: Sociological Journal 3
discussions.html:
Sociological Journal 3
SOCIOLOGY HONORS · WEEK 3 · JOURNAL

Prompt

Name one social fact you had never consciously noticed until this week.

Then run it through Durkheim's three criteria from The Rules of Sociological Method I, and show your work on each:

  • External. Did it exist before you? Will it outlast you? Who made it, if anyone?
  • General. Does it hold across a group, or only for you and the people you happen to know?
  • Constraining. This is the one that needs evidence. Give a specific occasion when you felt the resistance. Not a dramatic one. The ordinary friction you met when you acted against it, or when you imagined doing so and decided not to.

What makes a strong entry

The best responses name social facts that are genuinely invisible. Laws and posted rules are social facts, but they are the easy case, because someone wrote them down and you already knew they were there. The interesting ones are the informal arrangements that structure behaviour without appearing in any written code: who speaks first, how close you stand, what you are expected to notice and expected to ignore, what counts as a reasonable amount of time before replying to someone.

A useful test before you commit: could you break this without breaking any rule anyone has ever stated? If yes, and something would still go wrong, you have found a good one.

Peer response

Read one classmate's entry and reply. Your reply must do one of these three things:

  1. Test the third criterion. They claimed constraint. Did they give evidence, or just assert it? If the evidence is thin, say what would have counted.
  2. Challenge the generality. Is this a social fact, or a habit of their particular family or friend group? That distinction is exactly what Durkheim's second criterion is for.
  3. Extend it. Name a related social fact their example reveals that they did not mention.

A reply that only agrees does not count. Neither does a reply that only compliments.

Scoring

Level Criteria
Full credit An invisible social fact, not a written rule; all three criteria addressed; specific evidence of constraint; a substantive peer reply doing one of the three moves above
Partial credit A written rule rather than an informal arrangement, or a criterion asserted without evidence, or a thin peer reply
No credit Missing, off-task, a summary of the lesson, or no peer reply

discussions.title: Sociological Journal 5
discussions.html:
Sociological Journal 5
SOCIOLOGY HONORS · WEEK 5 · JOURNAL

Prompt

Apply Berger's sociological consciousness to your own family. Choose one routine, practice, or expectation in your family life that you have never really questioned: a habit around meals, chores, holidays, who makes which decisions, how conflict gets handled, anything ordinary enough that you normally would not think about it at all.

Now look at it through sociological eyes:

  • What function does it serve? Not what anyone says it is for, but what it actually does.
  • Where did it come from? Does it reflect the norms of a particular culture, class, religion, or historical period, or a choice your own family made deliberately?
  • What would Aristotle say about it? Use his account of the household as the first school of authority and obligation.
  • What would Durkheim say about it? Use his account of social facts: external, general, and constraining.

Write 200 to 350 words. Do not summarize the lessons; use the concepts to illuminate what you actually observed.

What makes a strong entry

The best responses pick something genuinely small and specific: not "how my family shows love" but the particular Sunday-dinner seating arrangement, the particular way phones get put away at the table, the particular order in which siblings are allowed to speak at a family meeting. A routine you can describe in one sentence and then spend two hundred words analyzing is more useful here than a grand claim about "family values" that never gets specific enough to test against Aristotle or Durkheim.

A useful check before you submit: could a stranger, reading only your description, tell what function this routine actually serves? If your answer only restates what your family says the routine is for, look again for what it also does.

Peer response

Read one classmate's entry and reply. Your reply must do one of these three things:

  1. Test the Durkheim application. Did they show the routine is external, general, and constraining, or only assert it? If evidence is thin on any of the three, say what would count.
  2. Offer a different Aristotle reading. Does their routine look more like the authority relationship, the marriage relationship, or the procreative relationship as Aristotle describes them? Sometimes a routine fits more than one, and saying which one you would emphasize, and why, is a real contribution.
  3. Extend it. Name a related family routine their example brings to mind that they did not mention, and say what function it might serve.

A reply that only agrees does not count. Neither does a reply that only compliments.

Scoring

Level Criteria
Full credit A specific, genuinely unexamined routine; both thinkers applied with real reasoning, not just named; a substantive peer reply doing one of the three moves above
Partial credit A routine described too broadly to test against either thinker, or a thinker named without real application, or a thin peer reply
No credit Missing, off-task, a summary of the lessons, or no peer reply

discussions.title: Sociological Journal 7
discussions.html:
Sociological Journal 7
SOCIOLOGY HONORS · WEEK 7 · JOURNAL

Prompt

Identify one relationship in your life that is clearly Gemeinschaft in character: personal, total, based on mutual obligation and a shared identity you did not choose. Identify a second relationship that is clearly Gesellschaft in character: contractual, partial, instrumental, entered and exited by agreement. Describe both precisely, using Tönnies's vocabulary rather than restating the dictionary definitions.

Now identify a third relationship that is genuinely ambiguous: it carries real features of both types at once. Say what makes it ambiguous, specifically. A relationship that just happens to fall somewhere in the middle is not the same as one that shows a real mixture, and the second is what this entry is asking for.

For each of your three examples, add one phrase naming which of Durkheim's forms of solidarity (Week 4) would classify the same relationship, mechanical or organic, and say in one sentence whether Tönnies's vocabulary and Durkheim's line up here or cut the relationship differently. This is the week's cross-reference, and it belongs in the graded work, not only in the reading.

Finish by saying whether the ambiguity in your third example feels, on reflection, like a strength of that relationship or a weakness. Write 200 to 350 words total.

What makes a strong entry

The best entries pick a genuinely ambiguous third case rather than a lazy compromise. "My friendship with my roommate" is not automatically ambiguous just because friendship sounds warm; it only counts if you can point to specific Gesellschaft-like features (it was chosen, it could end without consequence, some part of it is transactional) sitting alongside specific Gemeinschaft-like features (real mutual obligation, no exit clause either party would actually use). A relationship that is simply hard to classify because you have not thought about it carefully is not the same as one that is hard to classify because it genuinely straddles the line.

A useful test before you commit to your third example: can you name one moment where the relationship behaved like Gemeinschaft, and a separate moment where it behaved like Gesellschaft? If you can point to both moments, you have found a strong example.

Peer response

Read one classmate's entry and reply. Your reply must do one of these three things:

  1. Test the ambiguous case. Does their third example actually show a mixture, or does it lean entirely one way once you look closely? If it leans one way, say which way and why.
  2. Challenge the Durkheim cross-reference. Do their Durkheim and Tönnies classifications actually line up the way they claim, or does one of the three examples reveal a place where the two vocabularies cut differently?
  3. Extend it. Name a related relationship from your own experience that fits the same category as one of theirs, and say what it adds.

A reply that only agrees does not count. Neither does a reply that only compliments.

Scoring

Level Criteria
Full credit A genuine Gemeinschaft example and a genuine Gesellschaft example, both precisely described; a third example that shows real mixture rather than mere uncertainty; the Durkheim cross-reference addressed for all three; a substantive peer reply doing one of the three moves above
Partial credit An ambiguous third example that is not actually mixed, or the Durkheim cross-reference skipped or thin, or a thin peer reply
No credit Missing, off-task, a restatement of the lesson's definitions with no personal examples, or no peer reply
